lmsArticle.title: System Design Requirements and Constraints: Ask Better Questions Before You Draw
lmsArticle.subtitle: A practical framework for clarifying functional scope, non-functional targets, and trade-off boundaries in interviews.
lmsArticle.excerpt: In system design interviews, weak answers fail early because requirements are fuzzy. Strong answers start by turning vague prompts into explicit functional scope, measurable non-functional targets, and clear trade-off boundaries before any architecture diagram appears.
lmsArticle.content:
## Scenario context

In system design interviews, weak answers fail early because requirements are fuzzy. Strong answers start by turning vague prompts into explicit functional scope, measurable non-functional targets, and clear trade-off boundaries before any architecture diagram appears.

> **TLDR**: If you clarify requirements well, the architecture almost chooses itself.



```architecture
{
  "version": 1,
  "title": "TLDR:** In sy…

This walkthrough focuses on **Why Requirement Clarity Is the Real Beginning of System Design**.

Before making a design choice, clarify:

- Slack assumed users were on reliable corporate networks.
- When mobile users on 3G hit the app in 2015, 40% quit within 30 seconds.
- The non-functional requirement "must load in under 3 seconds on 3G" was never written down.

**Concepts in play:** system-design-hld-architectures, caching, consistency-replication, stack-and-queue-data-structures

## Stage 1 — The Requirement Stack: Functional, Non-Functional, and Business Constraints

- A reliable way to avoid chaos is to classify requirements into layers.
- Functional requirements answer "What should the system do?" Examples: - Users can create short links.
- - Users can view a personalized feed.
- - Drivers can request rides and track status.

*Applies **system-design-hld-architectures** to the decision above.*

**Observable outcome:** - Drivers can request rides and track status.

## Stage 2 — A Practical Requirement Interview Script You Can Reuse

- Candidates often ask: "What exactly should I ask first?" Use a short script in this order: 1.
- Define the primary user journey.
- Define strict consistency boundaries.
- Here is a reusable checklist table: This script works because it does not require perfect numbers.

*Applies **caching** to the decision above.*

**Observable outcome:** Here is a reusable checklist table: This script works because it does not require perfect numbers.

## Stage 3 — Deep Dive: Translating Requirements Into Enforceable Design Decisions

- Requirement gathering is useful only if it drives specific architecture decisions.
- The translation step is where many interviews are won.
- The Internals: Requirement-to-Component Mapping Every clarified constraint should map to one or more design mechanisms.
- - Low read latency target - cache layer, denormalized read model, or edge routing.

*Applies **consistency-replication** to the decision above.*

**Observable outcome:** - Low read latency target - cache layer, denormalized read model, or edge routing.

## Stage 4 — Requirement Funnel: From Vague Prompt to Defensible Architecture

- architecture { "version": 1, "title": "Requirement Funnel: From Vague Prompt to Defensible Architecture - Subsystem Overview", "description": "Decoupled system architecture isolating ingress, stateless logic, and persis…
- If the interview starts drifting, return to the funnel and show what changed in assumptions.
- 📊 Requirements Classification Tree This classification tree shows how any system requirement maps to one of three categories.
- Functional requirements define what the system does — user actions, core operations, and API boundaries; non-functional requirements define how well it must do it — latency targets, availability SLOs, and consistency le…

*Applies **stack-and-queue-data-structures** to the decision above.*

```mermaid

```

```

flowchart TD
    A[Vague interview prompt] --> B[Clarify functional scope]
    B --> C[Capture non-functional targets]
    C --> D[Set constraints and assumptions]
    D --> E[Define out-of-scope boundaries]
    E --> F[Map constraints to components]
    F --> G[Present architecture with trade-offs]

```

**Observable outcome:** Functional requirements define what the system does — user actions, core operations, and API boundaries; non-functional requirements define how well it must do it — latency targets, availability SLOs, and consistency le…

## Stage 5 — Real-World Applications: Notification, Feed, and Checkout Systems

- The same requirement framework applies across very different domains.
- Notification platform: - Functional: send notification, view delivery status.
- - Non-functional: near-real-time delivery for push, eventual for email.
- - Constraints: provider rate limits, regional SMS regulations.

*Applies **system-design-hld-architectures** to the decision above.*

**Observable outcome:** - Constraints: provider rate limits, regional SMS regulations.

## Stage 6 — Practical Example: Requirement Breakdown for "Design a Chat System"

- Suppose the interviewer says: "Design WhatsApp." A structured response starts with narrowing: - Phase 1: one-to-one messaging only.
- - Exclude group chat, media compression, and end-to-end encryption details from MVP.
- Then define measurable assumptions: Now architecture decisions follow naturally: 1.
- Per-conversation ordering requirement - partition messages by conversation ID.

*Applies **caching** to the decision above.*

**Observable outcome:** Per-conversation ordering requirement - partition messages by conversation ID.

## End-to-end outcome

After working through the stages, you should be able to explain:

- - Requirements are architecture inputs, not interview formalities.
- - Functional, non-functional, and business constraints should be separated explicitly.

## Alternatives considered

### Decision Guide: Which Requirement Style Fits the Interview Prompt?

This decision table helps you adapt your questioning style without sounding scripted.


## Failure and degraded modes

### Trade-offs & Failure Modes: What Goes Wrong When Requirements Are Weak

- **Detection:** A strong candidate explicitly narrates these failure modes and shows how requirement discipline prevents them.
- **User or operator impact:** A strong candidate explicitly narrates these failure modes and shows how requirement discipline prevents them.

seriesList.description: Master the core of computer science. This series demystifies Data Structures and Algorithms, from Big O to graph theory. Learn to write efficient, scalable code and ace your technical interviews with confidence.

seriesList.name: Machine Learning Fundamentals
seriesList.description: This series breaks down complex mathematical theories and algorithms into simple, intuitive explanations with practical examples, making AI accessible to everyone from beginners to aspiring data scientists.

seriesList.name: Architecture Patterns for Production Systems
seriesList.description: High-level design is only half the battle; the other half is surviving production. This series explores the architectural patterns required to build resilient, scalable, and maintainable systems. We dive into the trade-offs of microservices vs. monoliths, event-driven architectures, caching strategies, and data consistency models. Each post focuses on proven patterns that solve common bottlenecks in high-traffic production environments, helping you move from "it works on my machine" to "it works at scale."

seriesList.name: Low-Level Design Guide
seriesList.description: Good architecture is built on a foundation of solid low-level design. This series is a deep dive into the "micro" side of software engineering—focusing on class design, object-oriented principles (SOLID), and tactical design patterns. We explore how to translate requirements into clean, maintainable code, handle concurrency at the component level, and define clear interfaces. Whether you're preparing for LLD interviews or looking to sharpen your day-to-day coding craftsmanship, this guide provides the blueprints for building modular software.

seriesList.name: Architecture Patterns for Production Systems
seriesList.description: High-level design is only half the battle; the other half is surviving production. We dive into the trade-offs of microservices vs. monoliths, event-driven architectures, caching strategies, and data consistency models. Each post focuses on proven patterns that solve common bottlenecks in high-traffic production environments, helping you move from "it works on my machine" to "it works at scale."

seriesList.name: How It Works: Internals Explained
seriesList.description: Ever wondered what actually happens when you trigger a function, commit a transaction, or deploy a container? This series peels back the layers of abstraction to explore the low-level mechanics of modern technology. From database engines and operating system internals to the hidden plumbing of distributed systems, we dive deep into the source code and architectural designs that make complex software work. No magic, just engineering.

seriesList.name: Software Engineering Principles
seriesList.description: Writing code is easy; engineering software that lasts is hard. This series explores the core philosophies and mental models that define professional software development. We go beyond syntax to discuss the timeless principles of modularity, abstraction, testing strategies, and technical debt management. Whether we’re discussing the Zen of Python or the rigors of formal verification, this series provides a high-level perspective on how to think like an engineer, not just a coder.
